lines.text: A velocity can change even on a straight road, and the signs tell you which way the particle moves. A sketch or a few measured quantities can reveal displacement, distance and acceleration without following every instant of the journey.

Choose a positive direction, then let s be signed displacement, u and v initial and final velocities, a constant acceleration, and t elapsed time. For straight line motion at constant acceleration, use v equals u plus a t, s equals u t plus one half a t squared, s equals one half open bracket u plus v close bracket t, or v squared equals u squared plus two a s. Select the equation containing the known values and the quantity sought. On a displacement time graph, gradient gives velocity. On a velocity time graph, gradient gives acceleration and signed area gives displacement. On a speed time graph, area gives total distance. On an acceleration time graph, signed area gives change in velocity. A horizontal acceleration time line corresponds to a straight velocity time line and a quadratic displacement time curve. Use g equals nine point eight metres per second squared where gravity is involved, with a sign set by your chosen positive direction. A fifth form, s equals v t minus one half a t squared, follows from s equals one half open bracket u plus v close bracket t with u equals v minus a t, none of the five is printed in the paper.

These equations and graphs describe the same motion, a constant velocity time gradient is the acceleration, and the area under that line produces s equals u t plus one half a t squared. If the line crosses the time axis, split the journey there to calculate distance.

Choose one positive direction and keep displacement, velocity and acceleration signed. Use a suvat equation only within an interval of constant acceleration. Displacement time gradient is velocity, velocity time gradient is acceleration. Velocity time signed area is displacement, speed time area is distance. Acceleration time signed area is change in velocity. Learn all five equations, including s equals v t minus one half a t squared, the paper does not give them.
Why does a velocity time graph crossing below the time axis require two different area calculations for displacement and distance?

On a velocity time graph, what does the signed area between the graph and the time axis give? Displacement Distance travelled Acceleration Final velocity ay Velocity multiplied by time gives signed displacement. Area below the axis subtracts from the total, adding its magnitude instead would contribute to distance.
State what the gradient of a velocity time graph represents.
The gradient is change in velocity divided by change in time, acceleration. Displacement comes from signed area under the graph.
Think of rise divided by run.
The vertical axis measures velocity and the horizontal axis measures time.
Write the units of the gradient.

A velocity time graph has a straight line from zero to four metres per second over two seconds, then a straight line to minus two metres per second over the next three seconds. State the displacement over the five seconds.
The first triangle has area four m. The second trapezium has signed area three m, giving seven m, adding the area below the axis positively gives distance, not displacement.
Areas below the time axis have a negative sign.
Split the graph into the first triangle and the later trapezium.
Use average velocity times time for each straight segment.
Explain how displacement, velocity, speed and acceleration can be read from displacement time, velocity time, speed time and acceleration time graphs.
A graph gradient compares change in the vertical quantity with time, an area multiplies the vertical quantity by time. Keep the sign for vector quantities.
Match the vertical axis to the quantity.
Use slope for rates of change and area for accumulated change.
Distinguish signed velocity from nonnegative speed.
A particle has velocity minus three metres per second and constant acceleration minus two metres per second squared. Explain what happens to its speed over the next second and why.
Using v equals u plus a t gives v equals minus five metres per second after one second. The speed is its magnitude, five metres per second, so negative acceleration does not by itself mean slowing.
Keep direction signs separate from speed.
Use v equals u plus a t for one second.
Compare the magnitudes of the initial and final velocities.
Sketch a velocity time and a displacement time graph for a particle starting with positive velocity and moving with constant negative acceleration, until it stops. Label each graph's key features.
Constant negative acceleration gives a linearly decreasing velocity. Because displacement gradient equals velocity, the displacement curve rises but flattens to a horizontal tangent at rest.
A constant acceleration fixes the velocity graph gradient.
Velocity is the displacement graph gradient.
Mark the stop where velocity reaches zero.

A particle starts from rest at t equals zero and moves in a straight line. Its acceleration is four metres per second squared for zero is less than or equal to t is less than three, zero for three is less than or equal to t is less than five, and minus six metres per second squared for five is less than or equal to t is less than or equal to eight, where t is measured in seconds. part a, Sketch the speed time graph for zero is less than or equal to t is less than or equal to eight, labelling the speed at t equals three, t equals five and t equals eight and the time at which the particle is momentarily at rest. part b, Hence find the total distance travelled during the eight seconds.

Each interval of constant acceleration adds its signed area to the velocity, giving zero gives twelve, then twelve, then twelve gives minus six. Speed is the magnitude, so the speed time graph touches zero at t equals seven seconds and rises again, its total area is the distance, fifty seven metres, whereas the displacement is only fifty one metres.
The acceleration graph tells you how the velocity changes, not what it is, so you also need the starting value.
Work along the motion one interval at a time, carrying the end velocity of each interval into the next, then take magnitudes to get speed.

On five is less than or equal to t is less than or equal to eight write v equals twelve minus six open bracket t minus five close bracket and solve v equals zero to find where the graph meets the time axis.

A particle moving in a straight line has velocity five metres per second at t equals zero. Its acceleration time graph is horizontal at three metres per second squared for zero is less than or equal to t is less than four and horizontal at minus two metres per second squared for four is less than or equal to t is less than or equal to nine, with t in seconds. Find its velocity at t equals nine seconds.

The signed areas are three times four equals twelve and minus two times five equals minus ten, a total change in velocity of plus two metres per second, so v equals five plus two equals seven metres per second. Quoting two metres per second treats the area as the velocity itself rather than the change in it, and twenty seven metres per second adds the area below the time axis positively.
An area under an acceleration time graph has the units of a velocity, but it measures a change.
Find the area of each rectangle with its own sign, then combine both with the initial velocity.
The second rectangle lies below the time axis, so its area is minus two times five.

A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration a. Its velocity is u at time zero and v at time t, and its displacement over that time is s. By considering the area under its velocity time graph, show that s equals u t plus one half a t squared.

Displacement is the signed area under a velocity time graph. For constant acceleration that area is a rectangle of area u t plus a triangle of area one half t open bracket v minus u close bracket, and the gradient of the line gives v minus u equals a t, which turns the triangle into one half a t squared.
The command word Show that means every line of the argument must appear, ending at the printed result.
Displacement is the area under the velocity time graph, and the gradient of that graph is the acceleration.
Draw the straight line from open bracket zero, u close bracket to open bracket t, v close bracket and cut the region beneath it into a rectangle and a triangle.
three Kinematics of a particle moving in a straight line.
In one breath.

A particle moving in a straight line has signed displacement, velocity and acceleration once you choose a positive direction. With constant acceleration, a small set of equations links these quantities, graph gradients and areas give the same motion information visually.
Key ideas.

Take one direction as positive throughout. Displacement s is the signed change in position, whereas distance is the total length travelled. Velocity is the rate of change of displacement, speed is the nonnegative magnitude of velocity. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. A negative acceleration points in the negative chosen direction, whether the particle slows down depends on the sign of its velocity.
Use u for initial velocity, v for final velocity, a for constant acceleration and t for elapsed time. The constant acceleration, or suvat, equations are.
v equals u plus a t, s equals u t plus one half a t squared, s equals one half open bracket u plus v close bracket t, v squared equals u squared plus two a s.

The third equation uses average velocity, open bracket u plus v close bracket over two, which is valid here because velocity changes linearly. These equations apply within an interval of constant acceleration. For free fall near Earth, use g equals nine point eight metres per second squared and choose downward or upward as positive before assigning the sign of a.

A fifth equivalent form, s equals v t minus one half a t squared, is often quicker when the final velocity rather than the initial one is known, putting u equals v minus a t into s equals one half open bracket u plus v close bracket t gives s equals one half open bracket two v minus a t close bracket t equals v t minus one half a t squared. None of these equations is printed in the examination paper, so all five have to be recalled.

A displacement time graph has velocity as its gradient. On a velocity time graph, gradient is acceleration and signed area between the line and time axis is displacement. Area below that axis is negative. A speed time graph has nonnegative height and its area is distance. On an acceleration time graph, signed area gives change in velocity. Constant acceleration appears as a horizontal acceleration time line, a straight velocity time line, and a quadratic displacement time curve. When velocity reaches zero, the displacement time graph has a horizontal tangent, the particle may then reverse direction.

Here the line crosses the time axis at t equals four seconds, where the particle is momentarily at rest and then reverses. The shaded region above the axis has area plus sixteen metres and the region below has area minus nine metres, so the displacement is sixteen minus nine equals seven metres while the distance adds the magnitudes, sixteen plus nine equals twenty five metres.

The shaded rectangle under this acceleration time graph has area three times five equals fifteen metres per second, which is the change in velocity over the five seconds and not the velocity itself, add it to u to get v. The same constant acceleration makes the velocity time graph a straight line of gradient three and the displacement time graph a quadratic curve.
Method.
Sketch a direction arrow and record known values with signs and units, u, v, a, s, t.

Choose an equation containing the unknown and known quantities, leaving out the one quantity you do not have. If motion has stages, treat each constant acceleration stage separately and carry the final velocity into the next stage.
Substitute signed values before simplifying. If an equation gives v squared, check both possible signs of v against the motion.
For a graph, use a gradient for a rate of change and an area for an accumulated change. Split areas at every change of slope or crossing of the time axis.
Give a unit, sensible significant figures and a contextual check. A displacement can be negative, a distance cannot.
Worked example.

A particle starts at three metres per second and accelerates at two metres per second squared for four seconds. Find its final velocity and displacement. Take the initial direction as positive. Here u equals three, a equals two and t equals four. v equals u plus a t equals three plus two open bracket four close bracket equals eleven metres per second. s equals u t plus one half a t squared equals three open bracket four close bracket plus one half open bracket two close bracket four squared equals twenty eight metres. The positive answers agree with motion continuing forwards and speeding up.
Traps.

Trap, Treat a negative acceleration as proof that speed decreases. Why it's wrong, A particle moving in the negative direction speeds up if acceleration is also negative. Instead, Compare the signs of velocity and acceleration.

Trap, Add every velocity time area positively to obtain displacement. Why it's wrong, Area below the time axis represents negative displacement. Instead, Use signed areas for displacement and absolute areas for distance.
Trap, Use a suvat equation across a change in acceleration. Why it's wrong, Its derivation assumes one constant value of a. Instead, Split the motion into constant acceleration intervals.
Exam technique.

For Find or Calculate, show the equation, substitution and result with units. For Sketch, label axes, intercepts and the sign or shape of the gradient, a straight velocity time line signals constant acceleration. For Explain, name the graph operation and the physical quantity it produces. If a particle turns, find the time when v equals zero before calculating total distance. With g equals nine point eight metres per second squared, quote a calculated result to two or three significant figures.
Turning an acceleration time graph into a speed time graph.
Write down the initial velocity, the acceleration graph on its own cannot tell you it.
Take one interval at a time and add that interval's signed area to the velocity at its start.
Plot those velocities and join them, constant acceleration gives a straight segment, zero acceleration a horizontal one.
Mark every time at which the velocity changes sign, solving v equals zero for it.
Reflect the parts below the axis upwards to turn velocity into speed, then read distance as the total area under the speed time graph.

Pearson's guidance for this topic says graphical solutions to problems may be required, covering displacement time, velocity time, speed time and acceleration time graphs. W M E zero one papers do ask for speed time graphs to be sketched on given axes, and their mark schemes credit either a gradient read from the sketch or v equals u plus a t, so a labelled sketch earns marks even when an equation supplies the number.
Self test.
Three checks.
A particle has u equals minus four metres per second and a equals minus two metres per second squared. Is it speeding up or slowing down? Speeding up, velocity and acceleration have the same sign.

An acceleration time graph is horizontal at minus two metres per second squared for six seconds and the particle starts at nine metres per second. Find the velocity at t equals six seconds. The signed area is minus twelve metres per second, so v equals nine minus twelve equals minus three metres per second.

For that motion, find the displacement and the distance over the six seconds. Velocity is zero at t equals four point five seconds, displacement equals one half open bracket four point five close bracket times nine plus one half open bracket one point five close bracket open bracket minus three close bracket equals twenty point two five minus two point two five equals eighteen metres, distance equals twenty point two five plus two point two five equals twenty two point five metres.
